abstract.t: This document specifies the UDP protocol between the J-Type server and its clients. It defines the packet header, the session handshake and keepalive, every game message, the way a snapshot is split into datagrams, and the rules a receiver applies to what it accepts. It is the reference for writing another client for a J-Type server.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: J-Type is a networked shoot'em up for up to four players. One server owns the game: it moves the ships, decides what the missiles hit, keeps the score and sends the world to every client. A client reads the keys, sends them, and draws what the server sends. This document describes the bytes they exchange.

The engine provides the datagram envelope and the session layer. The game puts one message in each GameData packet. The protocol is state based: the server repeats the whole world and the whole score at every step, and the events only announce a change that the state of the same step already carries.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Scope
section.t: This document covers version 1 of the protocol. It does not describe the rules of the game, the assets, the rendering, or the C++ API of the implementation. The values of the game, such as the points a Bydo is worth, are part of the game and not of the wire format.

section.name: Transport and Framing
section.t: The protocol runs over UDP . A datagram carries exactly one packet. IP fragmentation is avoided: a datagram MUST NOT exceed 1200 bytes including the packet header, so it fits in the usual 1500-byte Ethernet MTU after the IP and UDP headers.

UDP does not deliver, order or deduplicate datagrams. A receiver MUST tolerate loss, reordering and duplication. The protocol does not retransmit lost game messages: the next state makes up for a lost one, as described in .

All multi-byte integer fields are unsigned and encoded in little-endian order, least significant byte first. Floating-point fields are IEEE 754 binary32 values , also little-endian. A receiver MUST reject a non-finite floating-point field.

section.name: Packet Header
section.t: Every datagram starts with the 8-byte header of the engine. The fields are:

The magic number rejects traffic from another application before any parsing. A datagram whose magic, version or type is unknown, that is shorter than the header, or that is longer than 1200 bytes MUST be dropped silently. The sequence number is a counter of the sender for each peer, starting at 0, increased by one for each packet sent to that peer, session packets and game messages alike, and wrapping modulo 2^32. It lets the peer detect loss; the protocol does not acknowledge or retransmit game messages.

tr.td: u32 cookie, copied from the Ping

section.t: A Ping or a Pong MUST carry exactly 4 payload bytes; a Connect, a ConnectAck or a Heartbeat MUST carry none. A packet that breaks these rules MUST be dropped. The payload of a GameData packet is decoded as described in .

section.name: Session
section.t: The session layer keeps track of the peers and of their liveness. A client MUST NOT send a game message before its session is open, and a server MUST drop a game message that comes from an endpoint without a session.

section.name: Handshake
section.t: The client sends a Connect and waits for a ConnectAck. It repeats the Connect until the server answers, so a lost Connect or ConnectAck only delays the handshake. The server answers every Connect from a known or a new endpoint with a ConnectAck and a Connect resets the sequence number that the server uses for that endpoint to 0.

The server keeps at most 1024 sessions. A Connect from a new endpoint while the table is full is dropped without an answer. A session ends when the peer stays silent for 3000 ms; a Leave frees the player's slot at once, without waiting for the timeout.

section.name: Keepalive
section.t: Once the session is open, the client sends a Heartbeat every 500 ms. The server answers each Heartbeat with a Heartbeat, so the client keeps hearing from the server even when the game sends nothing. A peer MAY also send a Ping every 1000 ms; the peer answers with a Pong carrying the same cookie, and the sender measures the round trip.

Any valid packet from a known peer refreshes its session, not only a Heartbeat. A heartbeat interval is shorter than the timeout, so several heartbeats fit in one timeout and a single lost datagram does not end a healthy session.

section.name: Game Messages
section.t: A GameData payload holds exactly one game message. Its first byte is the message type; the fields follow, in the order of this document. A decoder MUST reject an empty payload, an unknown type, a field that runs past the payload, a value outside its range, and a payload with bytes left after the last field.

section.name: Entity State
section.t: A snapshot and a Spawn event carry entities in this 14-byte form:

tr.td: Identity of the entity for the whole game
Health points left, 0 for an entity without health
Ship of the player of slot 0
Ship of the player of slot 1
Ship of the player of slot 2
Ship of the player of slot 3
Missile of the player of slot 0
Missile of the player of slot 1
Missile of the player of slot 2
Missile of the player of slot 3
Ship or Bydo that was just destroyed
Eye of the boss, the part the players can hurt
Eye of the boss once it lost half of its health
Orb the boss fires at a player
Spit of a fan the boss fires
Pellet of the spread shot of the player of slot 0
Pellet of the spread shot of the player of slot 1
Pellet of the spread shot of the player of slot 2
Pellet of the spread shot of the player of slot 3
Power-up that gives the spread shot
Block of a wall that took a hit
Piece of the beam of a zapper

section.t: A type outside this table MUST be rejected. The id of an entity is stable while it exists; once it is destroyed, the server may give the same id to a new entity. A receiver MUST therefore treat a Destroy event or the disappearance of an id from a snapshot as the end of that entity, and a Spawn event as the start of a new one.

section.name: Join
section.t: The client sends a Join once its session is open, and repeats it every 500 ms until the server answers with a Welcome or a Full. A client that already holds a slot gets that slot in a new Welcome. A Join starts a new stream of inputs: the server forgets the last input step it accepted from the client.

section.name: Welcome
section.t: The server answers a Join with the slot of the player. A new client gets the first free slot, from 0 to 3; a client that already has a slot gets it again.
A slot outside 0 to 3 MUST be rejected.

section.name: Input
section.t: The client sends its input at each of its steps. The payload holds the keys held down and the step of the client. The server applies an input to the ship of the slot that owns the endpoint; the wire carries no slot, so a client cannot move another player's ship.

A bit outside 0x1F MUST be rejected. The client starts its tick at 1 and increases it by one for each Input it sends; the counter wraps modulo 2^32. The server keeps the last tick it accepted for the client, resets it on a Join, and drops an Input whose tick is not newer under the serial comparison of . The server applies the input to the ship during the next step, and gives its tick back in the Last input field of the snapshots it sends to that client.

section.name: Snapshot
section.t: The server sends a snapshot at each of its steps. A snapshot is the whole world: every entity the clients must draw. When the entities do not fit in one datagram, the server splits the snapshot into chunks, as described in ; every chunk carries the same tick, the same last input and the same counts.

The Last input field is the tick of the last Input the server accepted from the client the snapshot is sent to, or 0 before the first one. The ship of that client has moved with this input, so the client can draw its own ship from the snapshot moved again by the inputs it sent since.

tr.td: Tick of the last Input accepted from this client, 0 before the first
Number of datagrams of this snapshot, at least 1
The entities of this chunk, in snapshot order

section.name: Scoreboard
section.t: The server sends the scoreboard after the events of each step. It always holds the four slots, in order, so its size is fixed.

tr.td: 0 while the game runs, 1 once every player is out of lives, 2 once the boss is beaten
Four entries of 7 bytes, see below
The player is out of lives until the next game
The player quit or timed out

section.t: A state outside 0 to 3, a weapon outside 0 to 1 and a game over byte outside 0 to 2 MUST be rejected. The game over byte is 1 or 2 from the step the game ends until the server starts the next game.

section.name: Leave
section.t: The client sends a Leave when it quits. The server frees the slot at once, removes the ship, and tells the other clients with a PlayerDisconnected event and the next scoreboard. A client that never joined MAY send a Leave; the server ignores it.

section.name: Full
section.t: The server answers a Join with a Full instead of a Welcome when the four slots are taken. The client cannot play and stops.

section.name: Spawn
section.t: The server announces an entity that appeared since the previous snapshot. The event carries the whole entity, so a client that missed the snapshot can still create it. The snapshot of the same step contains the entity too.

section.name: Destroy
section.t: The server announces that an entity is gone since the previous snapshot. The snapshot of the same step does not contain its id anymore; a client that missed the event removes the entity when it sees that snapshot.

section.name: PlayerDisconnected
section.t: The server tells the remaining clients that the player of a slot left, either with a Leave or by staying silent past the session timeout. The scoreboard of the same step shows the slot as Left.
A slot outside 0 to 3 MUST be rejected.

section.name: ScoreEvent
section.t: The server announces that a player earned points. The points are already counted in the scoreboard of the same step, which remains the authority on the score.
A slot outside 0 to 3 MUST be rejected.

section.name: DeathEvent
section.t: The server announces that a ship or a Bydo was destroyed, and who destroyed it. This is a notification for sounds and effects: the snapshot and the scoreboard of the same step already show the consequence.

tr.td: Slot of the player, or 255 for a crash or a Bydo missile

section.t: The killer MUST be 0 to 3 or 255; any other value MUST be rejected.

section.name: GameOverEvent
section.t: The server announces that the game ended, because every player is out of lives or because the boss is beaten. The scoreboard of the same step has its game over byte at 1 or 2. The server sends the event once per game; it sends it again only when a new game ends.

section.name: PickUpEvent
section.t: The server announces that the ship of a player took a power-up. This is a notification for effects: the snapshot and the scoreboard of the same step already show the consequence.

tr.td: Slot of the player whose ship took it
Takes the next hit; the ship has 2 health points while it lasts
The spread shot, until the ship is destroyed

section.t: A slot outside 0 to 3 and a power-up outside 0 to 2 MUST be rejected.

section.name: Snapshots and Chunking
section.t: The game runs on fixed steps of 1/60 s on both sides. The server starts its tick at 0, increases it by one at each step, and wraps it modulo 2^32. A snapshot, the events of the step and the scoreboard all carry the tick of the step they describe.
After the 8-byte packet header and the 15-byte snapshot header, 14 bytes per entity fit in a datagram of at most 1200 bytes. Therefore a chunk carries at most 84 entities:

A snapshot of n entities is split into max(1, ceil(n / 84)) chunks, numbered 0 to chunk count minus 1. The chunk of index i carries the entities from i * 84 to min((i + 1) * 84, n) - 1, in snapshot order. The count field of the chunk is the number of entities it carries, so the last chunk may be shorter. A snapshot holds at most 64 chunks, or 5376 entities; a larger snapshot is not sent.
An empty snapshot is legal: the server sends one chunk with chunk count 1, index 0, entity count 0 and count 0. A client MUST treat it as an empty world, not as a missing snapshot.

A chunk is valid only when its chunk count is 1 to 64, its index is below its chunk count, its entity count is at most 5376, its chunk count is exactly the one the entity count implies, and its count is exactly the number of entities the index implies. A chunk that breaks one of these rules MUST be dropped. A client reassembles the chunks of one tick, drops a duplicated index, and discards a snapshot whose chunks disagree on the entity count or the chunk count. An incomplete snapshot is discarded when newer ones replace it; the next complete snapshot carries the whole world anyway.

section.name: Reliability and Ordering
section.t: The protocol has no acknowledgement and no retransmission of game messages. It relies on two properties:

ul.li: Every message that carries state carries the whole state of its kind: a snapshot is the whole world and a scoreboard is the whole score. A lost one is replaced by the next one, 1/60 s later.
An event only announces a change that the snapshot or the scoreboard of the same step already carries. A lost event delays a sound or an effect, and never changes the game.

section.t: Join is the only game message that needs an answer. The client repeats it every 500 ms until a Welcome or a Full arrives. Connect and Heartbeat are repeated by the session layer as described in .

Snapshots can arrive out of order. A client keeps the snapshots in the order of their tick, and draws the world a few steps behind the newest snapshot so it can interpolate between two known states. The number of steps of delay is a client choice; it does not change the wire format.

section.name: Comparing Ticks
section.t: A tick is a 32-bit counter that wraps. Two ticks are compared with serial number arithmetic : a is newer than b when the signed 32-bit value of a - b is positive. For example, 0 is newer than 0xFFFFFFFF, and 0xFFFFFFFF is not newer than 0. Two equal ticks are not newer than each other.

The server uses this comparison for the tick of an Input. It accepts the first Input of a client, then only an Input whose tick is newer than the last one accepted; a duplicated or reordered Input is dropped. A Join resets the comparison, so a client that starts its ticks again is accepted.

section.name: Validation and Error Handling
section.t: A receiver validates each layer in order and drops what it cannot accept. It MUST NOT crash, block or allocate without bound on a malformed or hostile datagram.

tr.td: The packet is not a GameData packet
The payload holds no message type
The type byte is not 1 to 13
A field ends after the payload
A slot, a type, a state, an input bit or a float is out of range
The payload goes on after the last field
The fields of a snapshot chunk do not agree with its entity count

section.t: The server drops a datagram whose header fails, then a game message that fails to decode, and counts it. It prints the count and the first reason at most once a second, so a flood cannot flood the log too. A game message from an endpoint without a session is dropped. An Input from an endpoint without a slot is ignored, and an Input whose tick is not newer than the last one accepted is ignored.

To bound the work of one receive call, the server handles at most 256 datagrams per call; the rest waits for the next call. It queues at most 256 events per step; an event past that is dropped, and the state still carries the change. Its incoming and outgoing datagram queues hold at most 1024 datagrams, and its session table holds at most 1024 peers.

A client applies the same strictness: it drops a datagram from another address than its server, a packet the header rejects, and a game message the decoder rejects. It keeps the snapshots in the order of their tick and never draws the world backwards, so a duplicated or late snapshot has no effect on the picture.

section.name: Example Exchanges
section.t: The following diagrams show the messages, not every heartbeat or ping. UDP may reorder, duplicate or lose any of them.

section.name: Joining a Game

figure.name: Join Exchange
figure.artwork: Client Server | | | Connect (0x80) ------------------------>| session opens | <------------------- ConnectAck (0x81) | | | | Join (type 1) ------------------------->| | <------------ Welcome (type 2, slot 2) | | | | Input (type 3, tick 0) ---------------->| each client step | <----------- Snapshot (type 4, tick 0) | each server step | <--------- Scoreboard (type 5, tick 0) |

section.t: The client repeats Connect until the ConnectAck, then repeats Join every 500 ms until the Welcome. If the four slots are taken, the answer is a Full (type 7) instead of a Welcome, and the client stops.

section.name: Playing a Step

figure.name: The Datagrams of One Server Step
figure.artwork: Server step tick = t: Snapshot, chunk 0 of 2, tick t (up to 84 entities) Snapshot, chunk 1 of 2, tick t (the remaining entities) Spawn, tick t, entity (an entity appeared) Destroy, tick t, id (an entity is gone) ScoreEvent, tick t, slot, points (a player earned points) DeathEvent, tick t, id, killer (a ship or a Bydo was destroyed) PickUpEvent, tick t, slot, kind (a ship took a power-up) GameOverEvent, tick t (the game ended) Scoreboard, tick t (the whole score, four slots)

section.t: Only the snapshot and the scoreboard are states. The events of a step are sent after the snapshot and before the scoreboard, all with the same tick. A client that misses them still sees their result in the state of the same step.

section.name: Leaving and Timing Out

figure.name: Leave Exchange
figure.artwork: Client Server Other clients | Leave (type 6) -------->| | | | frees the slot, destroys the ship | | PlayerDisconnected --->| | | Scoreboard, Left ------>| | | | | (no Leave, 3 s silent) | sweep: same events |

section.t: A client that closes without sending Leave is removed by the session timeout after 3000 ms. The remaining clients see the same PlayerDisconnected event and the same Left scoreboard. When no client is left, the server starts a new game for the next players.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The protocol has no authentication and no encryption. A player is identified by the source address of its datagrams, and a UDP source address can be written by anyone. Someone who knows the address of a player can send Inputs or a Leave in their name, and an Internet-reachable server can be filled with fake sessions or fake players until the four slots are taken. The protocol is meant for a game on a local network.

The server is authoritative: a client sends only the five input bits, its own tick and its own Join or Leave. It cannot set a position, a health, a score, a killer or a slot on the wire. The server computes the game from the inputs it accepts.

A receiver bounds what an incoming datagram can make it allocate: the packet size is limited to 1200 bytes, the snapshot entity count to 5376, the session table to 1024 peers, the datagram queues to 1024 entries, and the events of a step to 256. A malformed datagram is dropped and counted, and its processing never throws.

The server logs the address of a joining player and a rate-limited summary of rejected datagrams. It logs no payload and keeps no log file; an operator who needs more keeps the standard output or adds counters.
